> **Shawn Lane, CEO of Ottimate, discusses AP automation in dentistry**


**Q: How does accounts payable (AP) automation eliminate the busywork during busy periods such as back-to-school season?**


Back-to-school season doesn't hit corporate first. It hits whoever's answering the phone when a vendor asks why they haven't been paid. By the time it hits the AP lead's queue, it's not a task list anymore; it's a backlog that gets worse while they read it. The invoice count goes up, but the exception count goes up faster, because the invoices that come in during a busy stretch are disproportionately the ones that don’t match a PO, don’t match the format the system expects, or need a human to figure out which of 40 practices the cost belongs to.


Most Dental Support Organisations (DSO) invoices (60-70%) never had a PO to begin with. Practices order reactively: a handpiece breaks, someone runs out of impression material, they order it on the spot. Busy season doesn't create that problem. It just turns up the volume on what was already there.


So, when people ask what eliminates the busywork, the honest answer has less to do with AI as a category and more to do with whether the system can actually read that non-standard invoice, code it to the right practice profit and loss (P&L) without a person doing it by hand, and handle a one-to-many allocation when one vendor bill needs to be split across a hundred locations. That’s the specific, unglamorous work that eats an AP lead’s day during a spike. If a tool can do those three things, the busy work goes away.


Rules-based OCR that's only ever seen clean, PO-matched invoices doesn't fail quietly during a spike. It fails by rejecting the exact invoices that were already the hard ones. Rigid approval workflows mean more manual intervention. And operators will tell you the real cost shows up when an invoice just disappears into the system with no vendor notification, more than in any single one of those failure modes. Now someone’s chasing it down instead of processing the next 50.


Dental lab invoices are small-dollar and high-volume, so they’re usually the first category to pile up when the AP team is underwater. AP lead is a high-burnout role for that reason; it’s the busy stretches that wear people down because it’s when exceptions stack up faster than one person can clear them.


Software aside, here’s what the fixed version of an AP lead’s day looks like: Non-standard invoices get read the first time correctly. That’s the whole ask. They’re not managing exceptions all day; they’re reviewing, approving, and moving on. Ental lab invoices, which are small-dollar and high-volume, stop being a category that piles up because nobody has time for them. It’s a queue that doesn’t grow faster than a person can clear it.


**Q: Why is AP automation critical for back-office stability?**


Months of garbage piling up outside a practice because one invoice sat unprocessed and nobody at corporate could see it happening. That's what AP breaking looks like at a DSO. Waste and bio-waste vendors are licensed; unlike a supply vendor, there's no grace period if that invoice doesn't get paid. At that point it's not an AP story anymore. It's a practice manager explaining a compliance problem to a health inspector.


Dental labs are the other place this reaches the patient directly. If a lab isn’t getting paid, at some point it stops sending work back. That dysfunction travels that far more than people want to admit, and it’s almost never framed as an AP problem when it happens. It gets framed as a vendor relationship problem, or a scheduling problem, and the real root cost never gets named.”


There’s a scaling math problem underneath all of this, too. A DSO doesn't get to grow its AP headcount at the same rate it grows practices. The process has to hold at many times the volume with a fraction of the people. That's not a stretch goal; it's just what growth requires.


There's a quieter version of the same failure: a cost lands on the wrong practice's P&L, and now a practice manager is arguing with corporate over numbers that don't match what actually happened at their location. That's not a bookkeeping footnote. That's the moment people stop trusting the report and start keeping their own spreadsheet on the side.


Splitting one consolidated invoice across hundreds of practice P&Ls in the correct proportions asks more of a system than a simple line-item match. It requires the system to understand the relationship between the vendor, the contract, and the practices, not just read a number off a page. When a tool can’t do that, someone’s doing it by hand in a spreadsheet, and that’s exactly the kind of task that doesn’t scale and doesn’t get faster no matter how experienced the person is.


To be fair, AP automation does have real limits when it comes to back-office stability. A DSO’s underlying growth strategy stays untouched by it, and the judgment calls a controller makes about vendor relationships stay with the controller. Its actual contribution is narrower. Removing the operational fragility that comes from stability depending on one person never missing an invoice. That’s a real problem worth solving, and also only part of the picture.


**Q: How can finance teams use AP automation to have real-time visibility into their spending, price fluctuations, and fraud protection?**


Ask most VPs of finance at a DSO what they can see across practices, and you’ll get a confident answer about the top-line numbers and a much less confident answer about anything underneath that.


The purchasing manager negotiates contract pricing through a GPO. That’s real, hard-won pricing. The question nobody wants to answer directly is how often what was negotiated matches what gets invoiced. In my experience, the gap is more common than people expect, and when it’s caught, it becomes a corporate-level conversation months later. Nobody’s sitting there matching every gloves order against the GPO contract terms in real time. That requires the system to know the contract price and automatically flag the variance, and most setups don’t do that.


DSOs use blanket POs instead of one-off POs for vendors supplying exam gloves, paper goods, and other recurring orders. Matching against a blanket PO isn’t the same as a standard three-way match. You’re checking cumulative spend against a committed amount over time. If a system only knows how to do a standard match, blanket PO categories become a manual exception every time, which defeats the purpose of using a blanket PO in the first place.


Real spend control was never about catching everything before it happens. It's catching the pattern – a vendor's pricing shifting, a category drifting outside its normal range, the same supply item costing different amounts at different practices. That's visibility after the fact, fast enough to still act on it. Different from the illusion of catching it all upfront.


A DSO running hundreds of practices fields an enormous number of vendor calls asking about invoice or payment status. Every one of those calls is someone at corporate dropping what they're doing to look something up. Moving that to a vendor portal hands that time back.


Some larger DSOs want purchasing, receiving, and AP working as one system, not three. I tell a prospect which one they need by asking where their pain is. If it’s invoice processing and coding, that’s an AP automation conversation. If they don’t have real purchasing controls upstream, the AP tool alone won’t fix that. That’s a procure-to-pay conversation, and pretending otherwise just delays them finding the right fit.


**Q: If you’re talking to a VP of finance at a DSO who knows the process is strained but hasn’t done anything about it yet, what’s the one thing you’d tell them to go look at this week?**


One question tells you more than your whole AP dashboard: how many of your invoices never had a PO to begin with? Whatever that number is, that's how much of your process is running on reaction instead of control.
